hints: Focus on oxidation numbers rather than just atoms moving, as oxidation and reduction are about change in oxidation state.
Work out the oxidation state of chlorine in $\text{Cl}_2$, in $\text{HOCl}$ where O is -2 and H is +1, and in $\text{Cl}^-$.
Check if the same starting element splits into one product with a higher number and another with a lower number, and also check H and O to see if they change at all.
walkthrough:
**Recall what oxidised and reduced mean**

Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is a decrease in oxidation number.

Rule to use:
$$\text{increase in O.N. = oxidised, decrease in O.N. = reduced}$$

**Find oxidation numbers for chlorine**

In $\text{Cl}_2$, each Cl is 0 because it is an uncombined element. This is our starting point.

In $\text{HOCl}$, H is +1 and O is -2, so Cl must be +1 for the total to be 0. In $\text{Cl}^-$, Cl is -1.

**Compare start and finish for chlorine**

One Cl atom goes $0 \to +1$. That is an increase, so oxidised. The other Cl atom goes $0 \to -1$. That is a decrease, so reduced.

$$0 \to +1 \text{ (oxidation) and } 0 \to -1 \text{ (reduction)}$$

**Check hydrogen and oxygen do not change**

In $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, H is +1 and O is -2. In $\text{HOCl}$ and $\text{H}^+$, H is still +1 and O is still -2. So they are neither oxidised nor reduced.

This special case where the same element is both oxidised and reduced is called disproportionation, so chlorine is both oxidised and reduced.

options.A: Correct. Chlorine starts at 0 in $\text{Cl}_2$ and splits into +1 in $\text{HOCl}$ (oxidised) and -1 in $\text{Cl}^-$ (reduced). This is disproportionation.
options.B: Incorrect. It is true chlorine is oxidised ($0 \to +1$), but it is also reduced ($0 \to -1$ in $\text{Cl}^-$). This option misses the reduction half of the disproportionation.
options.C: Incorrect. Hydrogen stays at +1 throughout: +1 in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, +1 in $\text{HOCl}$ and +1 in $\text{H}^+$. With no change in oxidation number, it is neither oxidised nor reduced.
options.D: Incorrect. Hydrogen does not change oxidation state at all, so it cannot be described as oxidised. Students sometimes confuse H transfer (acidity) with oxidation, but here it is just proton release, not electron loss by H.
